3698.prule: Stress falls on one of the last two syllables and its position is stated to depend on the word's morphological make-up, not on syllable count or weight: an uninflected (bare) word 'usually' / 'mostly' takes final stress (kʰaˈdo 'rat', uˈsa 'dog', tʰaˈtʃi 'nail', kʰiˈda 'tooth', baˈtʰa 'shoot', bakʰaˈɾa 'seed'), otherwise penultimate (ˈpʰapʰa 'mother', ˈkʰɾĩtʃʰa 'think', pʰeˈpʰena 'fan'); an inflected word (stem + suffix, or stem + case/topic enclitics in Carlson's terms) 'usually' takes penultimate stress counted over the whole prosodic word, suffix/enclitics included (kʰɾĩˈʧa-ta 'a thought', meˈa-de 'in the jungle', wũ̯ẽˈn̆ã=ba 'woman=erg', toˈro=a 'snake=dat'; with two enclitics the first enclitic is stressed: wũ̯ẽn̆ãˈᵐba=ɾa, toro.ˈa=ɾa). With a single suffix this coincides with the stem-final syllable, but the sources do not state a stem-final rule and their data contradict one: Carlson's (120c)/(121c) stress an enclitic, and Greenfield's /kʰo-ˈja/ 'eat' (-ya FUT/citation) and /nũ-b-u̶-ˈa/ 'present progressive' are suffixed words with final stress (exceptions to the penult generalization as well). Greenfield states that bare-word stress 'varies' and that the conditioning factors are beyond her scope.

tn.quote: En general, el tono parece ser más importante que la intensidad (véase, por ejemplo, Rex y Schöttelndreyer 1973: 79) en la manifestación fonética del acento y ciertas observaciones de Loewen (1958: 20, nota 4) sugieren incluso la posibilidad de que el sambú sea una lengua tonal ... No obstante, por el momento, todos los autores coinciden en asignar a las lenguas la condición de acentuales ... él acento recae en la penúltima sílaba casi sin excepciones en saija y chamí ..., en tanto que en catío y sambú puede recaer lo mismo en la penúltima que en la última.
tn.translation: In general, pitch seems to be more important than intensity (see, e.g., Rex & Schöttelndreyer 1973: 79) in the phonetic manifestation of the accent, and certain observations of Loewen (1958: 20, n. 4) even suggest the possibility that Sambú is a tone language ... Nevertheless, for the moment, all authors agree in assigning the languages accentual status ... the accent falls on the penultimate syllable almost without exception in Saija and Chamí ..., whereas in Catío and Sambú it may fall on the penultimate or the final alike.

tn.note: Treated as accentual, not tonal, 'for the moment': free accent (penult or final in Catío; /ˈ/ in its inventory), pitch its chief cue; tone raised only for Sambú; no tonemes; forms accent-marked only.

No secondary stress, weight or tone is mentioned and 'acento' is not defined.

3700.dq: Kiembu has high (H) and low (L) tone. The tones are represented in lexical items across Kiembu lexicon on syllabic basis. [p. 32] ... It has been noted that tone has a significant role in distinguishing the meaning of words. [p. 33]
3700.dloc: Ch. 2 'Basic phonology and morphology of Kiembu', sec. 2.5 Tone, pp. 30-32, and sec. 2.6 Summary, p. 33
3700.prule: No word-stress rule. Kiembu is described as a two-tone (H/L) language with lexical tone (mbia /mbí↓á/ 'money' vs /mbìà/ 'rat'; ngiri /ngírí/ 'a thousand' vs /ngìrì/ 'caveat') and grammatical/word-class tone (aka /àká/ 'women' vs /ákà/ 'build'; kana /ká↓nà/ 'child' vs /káná/ 'deny'); after naming stress, tone and duration as the suprasegmentals of prominence, the source states that tone is the only suprasegmental feature in Kiembu, so no stress is recognised and no stress position is given.
3700.srule: Not mentioned in Mwaniki 2014 (ch. 2, sec. 2.2 and 2.5-2.6, pp. 24, 30-33 read): tone is described as 'the only suprasegmental feature in Kiembu'; no stress, primary or secondary, is described.
3700.quote: Hyman (1975) refers to stress, tone and duration as suprasegmentals of prominence. He states that these features are always present in all utterances and hence any utterance in any language is characterized by differing degrees of loudness, melody and rhythm. The suprasegmental feature found in Kiembu is tone. Tone plays a very significant role in bringing out a number of contrasts such as in lexical differentiation, in tense and aspect constructs. [p. 30] ... Mutahi (1977), states that Kiembu is a tonal language. He adds that, tone plays an important role in dialect classification. He also n…
3700.loc: Ch. 2 'Basic phonology and morphology of Kiembu', sec. 2.5 Tone, pp. 30-32, and sec. 2.6 Summary, p. 33
3700.idn: Kiembu (the Embu North, Embu West and Embu East regional varieties; Kimbeere excluded); data: Embu East, West and North districts, Embu County, Kenya; non-mobile old rural male informants sampled from the three regions; fieldwork years not stated (MA project dated November 2014)
3700.tone: Two-tone (H/L) language, tones assigned per syllable in lexical items; lexical minimal pairs and noun/verb pairs distinguished by tone (sec. 2.5, pp. 31-32); tone patterns also serve as a dialect-classification variable (LH in Embu North/West vs LHLH in Embu East, sec. 3.2.4, pp. 39-40, after Mutahi 1977). On stress the source says only, by exclusion, 'The suprasegmental feature found in Kiembu is tone' (p. 30) and 'tone, the only suprasegmental feature in Kiembu' (p. 33), immediately after listing Hyman's triad stress/tone/duration; it never uses the words stress or accent of Kiembu itself. Caveat on that exclusion: the same thesis treats vowel length as distinctive (sec. 3.2.3, p. 37: 'In Kiembu vowel length is distinctive'), so 'only suprasegmental feature' is a loose claim, which is why the record is coded tone or pitch accent rather than no word stress.

evidence_works.note: Mills's own Massenrempulu material is described on printed p. 109: 'a) Enrekang dialect: a partial (± 175 words) Swadesh list. The stress statement is made for the Mass. group over that material: 'In the material which I myself have heard, stress falls on the penultimate syllable; the verbal person markers produce exceptions to this rule, as in the other languages. The same morpheme structure conditions as in the others appear to apply to the Mass. group as well.' The 'exceptions' are the stress-neutral verbal person-marker suffixes described for the earlier languages (Makassarese, sec. 2.1.2.1g, printed p. 74: 'Nor does stress shift for the verbal person-marking suffixes'): printed p. 191 explains that with the '3d person marker' /-i/ 'the stress remains on the penult of the base', but the examples there are 'cited from my Duri data only, not from the other Mass. languages' (p. 190-191), the one Enrekang form (End. ditamuii, from RAP72) being a source that 'does not mark the stress'. No instrumental measurement; impressionistic penultimate stress on elicited wordlists.

(thesis p. 4) | l’accent de mot, qui en éton tombe toujours sur la première syllabe des thèmes. 3712.prule: Obligatory, culminative, demarcative word accent on the first (and only the first) syllable of the prosodic stem; the prosodic stem = the morphological stem, plus the consonant of a C-prefix when the stem is vowel-initial. Prefixes (noun-class, verbal) are unaccented, so the accent is stem-initial, not word-initial, and its position follows from morphological structure rather than from syllable count or weight. Phonetic correlate: onset-consonant length (C1 more than twice as long), not vowel length, pitch or intensity; vowel reduction is only a secondary correlate.
3712.srule: None at word level: the accent is culminative ('Every first and only the first syllable of a prosodic stem is accentuated'); no secondary or rhythmic stress is described. Only reduplicated stems carry two accentuated syllables ('reduplicated stems have two accentuated syllables'), reduplicated forms being treated as two stems, each stem-initially accented.

3712.tone: Eton is a two-tone language in addition to the accent. Thesis pp. 4-5, in source order: 'The recognition of accent is crucial for a successful description of the tone system of Eton. Accentuated syllables can carry two structural tones, unaccentuated syllables only one. There are two tone levels in Eton, low and high. These tones can combine in a falling pattern, a rising pattern and a downstepped high pattern. Structurally, three tones must be distinguished: low, high and dissimilating high.' Dictionary §8.3 p. 21: 'Outre les consonnes et les voyelles, les tons jouent un rôle distinctif en éton. L’éton distingue deux tons, un ton haut (marqué avec un accent aigu) et un ton bas (marqué avec un accent grave).' with minimal pairs ŋgàz ‘poil de poitrine’ vs ŋgáz ‘fil de fer’. Tone does not mark the accent; the accent's correlate is consonant length (thesis p. 22).

tn.quote: Accentuated syllables can carry two structural tones, unaccentuated syllables only one. There are two tone levels in Eton, low and high. These tones can combine in a falling pattern, a rising pattern and a downstepped high pattern. Structurally, three tones must be distinguished: low, high and dissimilating high. The opposition between structural low and high tones is equipollent. ... A syllable can be associated to one of five different tone patterns: low (a`), high (a'), low-high (a‡), high-low (aﬂ) and downstepped high (Êa').
tn.cite: Van de Velde, Mark L.O. (2006). A Description of Eton: Phonology, morphology, basic syntax and lexicon. PhD thesis, Katholieke Universiteit Leuven.
tn.note: Two tone levels (L, H) plus a morphotonemic dissimilating high; rising, falling and downstepped high are combinations, two tones only on accented (stem-initial) syllables; accent is consonant length.

tn.quote: Etulo is characterized as a register tone language with three contrastive level tones and two contour tones. The level tones comprise the high tone [ ́], the low tone [ ̀] and mid tone [−] while the contour tones include the falling [ ̂] and rising [ ̌] tones. The lexeme’s inherent tones may change in grammatical constructions. Two tone bearing units are identified; vowels and syllabic nasals. ... Unlike other tones, the rising tone has no distinctive function in Etulo. It is restricted to the word final position and is preceded by a high tone.

3716.dq: The first, the Marked Stress Hypothesis, is that primary word stress is marked in the lexicon. [...] Stress always appears on the rightmost non-schwa vowel of a word. The stressed syllable is always one of the last three syllables in the word.
3716.dloc: Preprint text dump sec. 1 Introduction (Marked Stress Hypothesis: 'primary word stress'), sec. 2.2 'Faetar stress' (rule and window) (foot analysis), sec. 4.1 (oxytone morphological classes), sec. 5 Conclusion; published version pp. 239-254 (sec. 1, 2.2, 4.1, 5). 3716.prule: Primary word stress is lexically marked, restricted to a right-edge three-syllable window (final, penult or antepenult). Surface generalization: stress falls on the rightmost non-schwa vowel, but Nagy argues schwa is the reduced reflex of any unstressed vowel (post-tonic vowels categorically schwa, pretonic variably), so what is stored is the stress position: one generalized trochee built at the right edge plus at most one lexically extrametrical final syllable. Position is not computable from syllable count or parity and is not weight-conditioned (open and closed syllables both stressable).
3716.srule: Not mentioned in Nagy 2000 (sec. 2.2-2.4, 4.1-4.3, 5 read in full): the analysis assumes a single right-edge foot per word ('If we assume that only one foot is built on each word (at the right edge)'), pretonic syllables unfooted; no secondary or rhythmic stress is described. Sportello 2006 (pp. 12-13) likewise gives one tonic syllable per word and calls all other syllables 'atone'.

3717.dq: Stress is contrastive on the syllable level. ... aban 'orphan' / ában 'laugh' (word-level minimal pair; the sheet never uses the phrase 'word stress' and describes no phrasal prominence)
3717.dloc: OPD sheet p. 3, section 'Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length)' (stress statement and minimal pairs); p. 3 'Conventions: Phonological' (/ɑ/ centralised in unstressed syllables); p. 3 'Conventions: Orthographic' (tone not written, stress written only when necessary); page 3.
3717.prule: Stress is phonemically contrastive and not positionally predictable: the sheet gives a stress-only minimal pair in disyllables (aban 'orphan' vs ában 'laugh', final/unmarked vs initial) and states no positional rule. The stressed syllable is the one whose vowel nucleus is longer and clearer (a phonetic correlate, not a predictor: the inventory has no length contrast), and the vowel /o/ is always stressed (the one stated regularity). Stress and pitch are separate phonemic units (Mecklenburg 1974 p. 144 chart, 'Stress v́ (stressed), v (unstressed is unmarked)'; 'Pitch cvc' (high pitch), cvc (low pitch is unmarked)').
3717.srule: Not mentioned in Mecklenberg 1992 OPD (4-page sheet read in full; p. 3 'Suprasegmentals' gives only contrastive stress, the phonetic cue, '/o/ is always stressed' and four disyllabic examples; áwón 'bird' is printed with two accents without any primary/secondary distinction; the p. 4 text is unmarked for stress).

3718.prule: Stress is lexically distributed within a right-edge three-syllable window, as in Castilian/Galician-Portuguese: words are oxytone (agudas: última sílaba tónica), paroxytone (llanas: penúltima), proparoxytone (esdrújulas: antepenúltima) or, with enclitic pronouns, pre-proparoxytone (sobreesdrújulas: cómpramulu); the position is marked per word by the tilde on Castilian-type conventions and is not derivable from syllable count or weight. Sub-regularity: words ending in a falling diphthong (au, ou, eu, ai, oi, ei) are final-stressed (falau, falei, pareceu, ademais, despois). Tonic/atonic monosyllable pairs contrast (dá/da, é/e, máis/mais, tó/to, sé/se).
